lead: A water supply is judged by a short list of measured numbers: how clear it is, what it contains, and whether bacteria are present. Each number is compared with a standard. Hardness is the one number that packs calcium and magnesium together, expressed as calcium carbonate, so any two waters can be compared. This chapter lists the parameters and units, gives the drinking-water limits, and shows the hardness calculation that examiners ask for.
prereq: You need: Unit 1, coordination compounds, for why EDTA binds Ca²⁺ tightly at pH 10; here titration is only a method.

sections.h3: The short list of measured numbers

blocks.text: Water quality is a set of measured numbers compared with a standard. Physical tests describe appearance: turbidity in NTU (nephelometric turbidity units), colour in Hazen units, odour as threshold odour number, and temperature in °C. Chemical tests give pH, TDS (total dissolved solids, mg/L), conductivity (µS/cm), chloride, sulphate, nitrate, fluoride and iron (each mg/L), dissolved oxygen, BOD (biochemical oxygen demand, mg/L) and COD (chemical oxygen demand, mg/L). Biological tests count coliform bacteria as MPN (most probable number) per 100 mL.
The BIS 10500 drinking-water standard gives an acceptable limit and a permissible limit. The permissible limit applies only when no better source exists.

sections.h3: Hardness is Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ in disguise

blocks.text: Hardness is the soap-consuming power of water, caused almost entirely by Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺. It is reported as if all these ions were CaCO₃, so one number compares any water.

blocks.where: H is hardness as CaCO₃ in mg/L; m is the mass concentration of the ion in mg/L; E is the equivalent weight of the ion (Ca²⁺ = 20, Mg²⁺ = 12); 50 is the equivalent weight of CaCO₃.

blocks.text: Units: 1 meq/L = 50 mg/L as CaCO₃; 1 ppm = 1 mg/L in dilute water; 1 °French = 10 mg/L as CaCO₃; 1 °Clark = 14.3 mg/L as CaCO₃.

Temporary hardness comes from bicarbonates of Ca and Mg and is removed by boiling. Permanent hardness comes from chlorides, sulphates and nitrates and needs softening (see 7.2). Total hardness is the sum of the two. Classification: soft below 60, moderately hard 60–120, hard 120–180, very hard above 180 mg/L as CaCO₃.

Hardness is measured by titrating with EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) at pH 10, buffered with ammonia. Eriochrome Black T forms a wine-red complex with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺; at the end point EDTA takes the ions and the colour turns blue. The EDTA volume gives total hardness. Only a few universities teach this chapter in full depth; the calculation matters more than instrument detail.

spec.title: From sample to verdict
spec.aria: A sample splits into physical, chemical and biological tests; the tests feed a comparison against BIS 10500 limits, and the chemical branch separately produces a hardness value in CaCO₃ units.

examples.question: A groundwater sample contains Ca²⁺ = 80 mg/L and Mg²⁺ = 24 mg/L, with no other hardness-causing ions. Find the total hardness as CaCO₃ in mg/L and in meq/L, and say whether it meets the BIS acceptable limit of 200 mg/L. Take equivalent weights Ca²⁺ = 20, Mg²⁺ = 12, CaCO₃ = 50.
steps: Ca²⁺ contribution = 80 mg/L × 50 ÷ 20 = 200 mg/L as CaCO₃.
Mg²⁺ contribution = 24 mg/L × 50 ÷ 12 = 100 mg/L as CaCO₃.
Compare: 300 is above the acceptable limit 200 but below the permissible 600, so the water is used only when no better source exists.
examples.answer: Total hardness is 300 mg/L as CaCO₃, equal to 6 meq/L; it fails the acceptable limit but stays within the permissible limit.
examples.check:
ca = 80
mg = 24
ca_h = ca * 50 / 20
mg_h = mg * 50 / 12
total = ca_h + mg_h
meq = total / 50
print(int(ca_h))
print(int(mg_h))
print(int(total))
print(int(meq))

traps: Reporting 80 mg/L Ca²⁺ as 80 mg/L hardness; you must convert with ×50 ÷ 20.
Using the molecular weight 100 of CaCO₃ instead of its equivalent weight 50.
Mixing temporary and permanent hardness; both are included in total hardness.
Forgetting the pH 10 buffer in EDTA titration; the end point becomes poor and the result wrong.
Treating the permissible limit as normal; it applies only when no alternative source exists.

quiz.q: Define turbidity and give its unit.
quiz.a: Turbidity is cloudiness from suspended particles; unit NTU.
It converts different ions to one common scale, so waters can be compared.

quiz.q: A water has Mg²⁺ = 48 mg/L only. Find hardness as CaCO₃.
Convert 250 mg/L as CaCO₃ to meq/L and °French.
pH 7.2, TDS 850 mg/L, hardness 320 mg/L as CaCO₃, fluoride 1.2 mg/L. Which values exceed acceptable but stay within permissible?
quiz.a: TDS (500/2000), hardness (200/600) and fluoride (1.0/1.5). pH 7.2 is within 6.5–8.5.

quiz.q: 100 mL sample needs 12 mL of 0.01 M EDTA. Find hardness as CaCO₃.
quiz.a: 12 × 0.01 = 0.12 mmol EDTA = 0.12 mmol CaCO₃; in 100 mL this is 1.2 mmol/L; × 100 mg/mmol = 120 mg/L.

beyond: Not for the exam. In a laboratory, the same numbers come from ion chromatography and atomic absorption spectroscopy, and coliform from membrane filtration. Water utilities log turbidity every few minutes because a sudden rise signals treatment failure. Search 'BIS 10500 drinking water specification' and 'EDTA hardness titration' for the primary documents.
